speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) since 2020, how many appeals have been received from Integrated Shield Plan insurance policyholders regarding their difficulties in making a claim that arises from the insurers’ definition of medical terminologies which diverge from how members of the public, laypersons and medical professionals may interpret the same terms; and (b) what recourse do affected policyholders have.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I declare that I am a medical doctor at a public hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met Clementi residents and fellow Singaporeans facing similar difficulties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Senior Parliamentary Secretary, first, when such wrong decisions are overturned on appeal, is there any requirement for the insurer to look back at earlier cases to see if there were other legitimate, valid claims that were incorrectly denied?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Second, I have met fellow Singaporeans whose IP insurers said the hospital bill needed particular words or phrases in order for a genuine claim to be allowed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This became a problem for some patients using their private insurance at a public hospital, because the public hospital billing format is standardised and may not match the insurer's technicalities and technical requirements.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What recourse do these patients have and would MOH be willing to look at this further to see if these are isolated cases or reflect a more systemic concern?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must not have a situation where a genuine claim cannot go through just because the customer is less literate, less eloquent and does not have access to their own legal team.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think these are legitimate concerns, especially if it involves laypersons who may not have access to legal advice on the matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Dr Tan also asked about the recourse that is available to the policyholders in such situations when there is difficulty in processing their claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have explained earlier the two platforms for the recourse that the policyholders have.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One, it is the Clinical Claims Resolution Process (CCRP) if the IP claim disputes are clinical in nature.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The other one is through FIDReC, where it includes other types of disputes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: FIDReC is an independent institution and it is set up specifically to handle disputes involving all types of retail, financial products and services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, they are best-placed to deal with these situations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is something very helpful to the policyholders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is also CCRP, as I mentioned earlier, which is administered by the Academy of Medicine Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It helps to deal specifically when there are issues relating to clinical matters pursuant to the IP plans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At the end of the day, I think the first step is to go back to the insurers and see how it can be resolved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Because each IP provider would have their own dispute resolution process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If there is, indeed, some difficulty and unfairness, they can go through these two dispute resolution processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Alternatively, if Dr Tan is aware of any specific cases, please refer them to us.
